The nitroglycerin process involved heating a mixture of nitrosyl chloride and potassium nitrate in a sealed vessel, which produced nitrosyl chloride and potassium nitrate. This mixture was then treated with sulfuric acid to convert the nitrosyl chloride into nitrosyl sulfate, which was then hydrolyzed to form nitrosyl nitrate. The nitrosyl nitrate was then hydrolyzed further to form nitrosyl sulfate, which was then hydrolyzed to form nitrosyl nitrate. This cycle repeated until the final product was pure nitrosyl nitrate.

The nitrosyl compounds were classified by their boiling points, which determined their stability and safety. Nitrosyl chloride was the most stable and least toxic, while nitrosyl sulfate was the most reactive and explosive. These compounds were used in artillery shells, naval shells, and naval mines, though their use was restricted by the Hague Convention of 1899, which banned the use of certain explosive materials in warfare.
